labels.answer: Position Indicating Device (PID) or Cone or Tube

cloze.text: The {{c1::atom}} is the smallest component of an element; it consists of a {{c2::nucleus}} and orbiting {{c3::electron(s)}}.
When atoms combine, they form a {{c1::molecule}}.
The nucleus is {{c1::positively}} charged, consists of {{c2::protons and neutrons}}, and contains nearly all of the atom's {{c3::mass}}.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Proton → P like Positive (positively charged); Neutron → N like Neutral (no electrical charge).

cloze.text: Orbiting electrons have a {{c1::negative}} charge and are held in {{c2::shells}} around the nucleus.
Electron shells are designated by the capital letters {{c1::K, L, M, N, O, P, Q}}.
The {{c1::K}} shell is closest to the nucleus and has the {{c2::highest}} binding energy (strongest bond); it is the most useful shell for medical imaging.
To remove an electron from its shell, the energy must be {{c1::equal to or greater than}} the {{c2::binding energy}} of that shell.
{{c1::Wilhelm Roentgen}} discovered X-radiation.
An ion pair is a {{c1::positive}} ion (the atom missing an electron) and a {{c2::negative}} ion (the ejected electron).
{{c1::Ionizing}} radiation is any type of radiation that is high in energy and can produce ions.
Both particulate and electromagnetic radiation are formed because of an {{c1::ionizing}} process.
{{c1::Particulate}} radiation involves particles that have {{c2::mass}} and travel in {{c3::straight lines}} at high speeds.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Particulate sounds like particle = has mass.

cloze.text: Particulate radiation cannot reach the {{c1::speed of light}}, and its particles may have a charge, except {{c2::neutrons}}.
Particulate radiation includes neutrons, protons, {{c1::electrons}}, and {{c2::beta particles}}.
cloze.extra: The book also lists "gamma particles" here, but gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation (the book lists them there too).

cloze.text: {{c1::Electromagnetic}} radiation consists of electric and magnetic fields of energy that move through space in a {{c2::wave-like}} motion.
Of the electromagnetic spectrum, only the {{c1::high-energy}} waves have ionizing capacity.
X-rays are powerful {{c1::electromagnetic}} energy capable of {{c2::penetrating}} substances (like teeth).
Wavelength is the distance between the {{c1::peaks (crests)}} of one wave and the next; it determines the {{c2::energy}} and {{c3::penetrating power}} of the radiation.
A longer wavelength = {{c1::low}} frequency, {{c2::lower}} energy, and less ability to penetrate objects.
A shorter wavelength = {{c1::high}} frequency and {{c2::higher}} energy.
X-rays are {{c1::invisible}}, travel at the {{c2::speed of light}}, and travel in {{c3::waves}}.
X-rays have no {{c1::mass}} and no {{c2::charge}}.
X-rays are {{c1::high}}-frequency, {{c2::short}}-wavelength radiation that can penetrate objects and can cause {{c3::changes in cells}}.
With {{c1::direct current (DC)}}, electrons flow in one direction; with {{c2::alternating current (AC)}}, electrons flow in two directions.
cloze.extra: Electricity is the power source for X-ray machines.

cloze.text: A circuit is the route the electrical current takes; the high-voltage circuit uses {{c1::65,000 to 100,000}} volts to provide high energy to produce X-rays.
A {{c1::transformer}} increases or decreases the voltage in an electrical circuit; types are {{c2::step-up}}, step-down, and {{c3::autotransformer}}.
The control panel displays on-off switches and the {{c1::milliamperage}}, {{c2::time}}, and {{c3::kilovoltage}} settings.
Amperage (mA) controls the {{c1::number}} of electrons; increasing mA produces {{c2::more}} electrons.
Dental machines operate at {{c1::5–8}} mA; mA controls the temperature of the {{c2::cathode filament}}.
Kilovoltage peak (kVp) is the peak voltage of an {{c1::alternating}} current; it determines the {{c2::speed}} at which electrons are propelled from the cathode.
kVp determines the {{c1::penetrating power}} of the X-ray beam, called beam {{c2::quality}}.
The {{c1::cathode}} is the {{c2::negative}} electrode; it is controlled by {{c3::milliamperage (mA)}} and is responsible for emitting electrons.
The {{c1::tungsten filament}} is the part of the cathode that emits electrons when {{c2::heated}}, forming an {{c3::electron cloud}}.
cloze.extra: Don't confuse the tungsten FILAMENT (cathode, emits electrons) with the tungsten TARGET (anode, where X-rays are made).

cloze.text: The {{c1::molybdenum (focusing) cup}} directs electrons toward the anode.
The {{c1::anode}} is the {{c2::positive}} electrode; it is controlled by {{c3::kilovoltage peak (kVp)}} and attracts electrons to produce X-rays.
The {{c1::tungsten target}} is the spot on the anode where electrons collide to generate X-rays.
The {{c1::copper stem}} conducts and dissipates excess heat.
The {{c1::lead glass vacuum housing}} encases the X-ray tube, contains the cathode and anode, and provides a {{c2::vacuum}} for X-ray production.
The {{c1::unleaded glass window}} allows X-rays to escape the tube and travel down the PID.
The {{c1::tubehead seal}} seals the tubehead to retain the {{c2::insulating oil}}, which aids in heat dissipation.
The {{c1::aluminum disks}} act as a filter, removing {{c2::long, weak (soft)}} wavelengths from the beam and so reducing patient exposure to non-diagnostic radiation.
The {{c1::collimator}} restricts the {{c2::size and shape}} of the X-ray beam, reducing patient exposure to unnecessary radiation.
The {{c1::metal housing (tube head)}} is the protective casing that houses the X-ray tube, transformers, and insulating oil, and assists with heat dissipation.
The {{c1::position-indicating device (PID)}} attaches to the tube head and directs the X-ray beam to the patient and image receptor; it comes in {{c2::cylindrical or rectangular}} shapes.
cloze.extra: Book says "film/sensor" — the exam says image receptor.

cloze.text: When the exposure button is pressed, electrons are propelled at high speed toward the anode's {{c1::focal spot}} within the {{c2::tungsten target}}.
When electrons hit the tungsten target, their {{c1::kinetic}} energy is transformed into {{c2::X-rays and heat}}.
A {{c1::photon}} is a bundle of energy.
{{c1::Primary}} radiation = photons leaving the X-ray tube that have not interacted with the patient's body or any other object.
X-rays are formed in the tube mainly by two mechanisms: {{c1::braking (bremsstrahlung)}} radiation and {{c2::characteristic}} radiation.
Bremsstrahlung radiation results when high-energy electrons come close to the {{c1::nuclei}} of the tungsten atoms.
In {{c1::characteristic}} radiation, electrons from the cathode dislodge electrons from the inner {{c2::K/L}} shell of the tungsten atoms.
In characteristic radiation, when inner-shell electrons are dislodged, electrons from other orbits {{c1::fill the space}} left by the ejected electron, and energy is produced.
Characteristic radiation is {{c1::not as significant}} a source of X-rays as braking radiation.
{{c1::Secondary}} radiation is created when the primary beam interacts with matter; it is {{c2::less}} penetrating than primary radiation.
X-rays can pass through the patient, be {{c1::absorbed}} by the patient, or be {{c2::scattered}}.
Photons that pass through an atom unchanged produce {{c1::densities}} on dental radiographs; if all photons pass through and reach the receptor, the image will be fully exposed ({{c2::dark}}).
{{c1::Scatter}} radiation is secondary radiation that results from deflection from the original path by interaction with matter; it is detrimental to {{c2::the patient and the provider}}.
Scatter radiation usually has a {{c1::longer}} wavelength than primary radiation and may cause {{c2::fogging}} of a radiographic image.

{{c1::Compton scatter}} (about {{c2::60}}% of interactions): a photon interacts with an {{c3::outer}}-shell electron, loses energy but continues to travel, and the electron is ejected (ionization occurs).
cloze.extra: Most interactions in dental X-rays are Compton because outer shells are easier to hit (their size and number of electrons).

cloze.text: {{c1::Photoelectric effect}} (about {{c2::30}}% of interactions): a photon interacts with an {{c3::inner}}-shell electron, is completely absorbed (transferring all its energy), and the electron is ejected (ionization occurs).
cloze.extra: Less common than Compton scatter because it requires interaction with the inner shells.

cloze.text: {{c1::Coherent scatter}} (about {{c2::8}}% of interactions): a photon interacts with an outer-shell electron but continues with {{c3::no loss of energy}}; no electron is ejected, so {{c4::no ionization}} occurs.
Radiation is measured in two systems: the {{c1::Standard (traditional)}} system and the {{c2::SI (Système International)}}, the newer system.

{{c1::Exposure}} is the quantity of ionization in air, measured at the skin surface before the radiation penetrates the tissues; units: {{c2::roentgen}} (standard) and {{c3::coulombs per kilogram (C/kg)}} (SI).
{{c1::Absorbed dose}} is the amount of radiation absorbed by an object (varies with the material); units: {{c2::rad}} (standard) and {{c3::gray (Gy)}} (SI).

{{c1::Dose equivalent}} is the absorbed dose adjusted for the biological damage potential of the type of radiation; units: {{c2::rem (roentgen equivalent in man)}} (standard) and {{c3::sievert (Sv)}} (SI).
cloze.extra: Some types of radiation cause more damage than others.

cloze.text: In the {{c1::direct}} theory, radiation damages the cell's protein, lipid, carbohydrate, and {{c2::DNA}} molecules and causes cell death.
In the {{c1::indirect}} theory, radiation interacts with the cell's {{c2::water}} content and produces {{c3::free radicals}}.
Free radicals are mostly {{c1::H and OH}}; they are highly unstable, interact with each other, and produce toxins such as {{c2::hydrogen peroxide (H2O2)}}.
The indirect theory accounts for about {{c1::2/3}} of radiation-induced biologic damage, proportional to body water content (the body is {{c2::60–80}}% water).
Highly radiosensitive cells are {{c1::immature}}, {{c2::quickly dividing}}, and a younger person's cells.
Less radiosensitive cells are {{c1::highly specialized}}, mature, and {{c2::slowly}} dividing.
The most radiosensitive part of a cell is the {{c1::DNA and chromosomes}}.
{{c1::All}} ionizing radiation is harmful and produces biological changes in living tissues.
Exposure of the {{c1::entire body}} results in more severe biological effects than {{c2::localized}} exposure.
{{c1::Short-term}} effects may occur minutes, hours, or weeks after exposure; they are {{c2::not present in dentistry}} because of the low doses.
cloze.extra: High doses can cause nausea, diarrhea, fever, hair loss, and death.

cloze.text: {{c1::Long-term}} effects may occur months, years, or decades after exposure; low doses over long periods may cause {{c2::cancer}}.
A {{c1::somatic}} effect is injury to the {{c2::person being affected}}; it follows a {{c3::nonlinear, threshold}} dose-response (examples: cataracts and cancer).
A {{c1::genetic}} effect injures {{c2::future generations}} (damage to reproductive cells); it follows a {{c3::linear, non-threshold}} dose-response, so even small doses may cause mutations.
In a {{c1::stochastic}} effect, the {{c2::probability}} of the effect increases with dose, but its {{c3::severity}} is not dose-dependent (an "all-or-none" effect, e.g. cancer).

In a {{c1::non-stochastic (deterministic)}} effect, the {{c2::severity}} of the effect depends directly on the dose received and there is a {{c3::threshold}} dose (e.g. hair loss, decreased fertility).
Natural sources of radiation include {{c1::radon}}, {{c2::cosmic}} radiation, and {{c3::terrestrial}} radiation.
{{c1::Radon}} is a gas released from the ground by decaying material; it penetrates every aspect of our environment (house, soil), combines with dust, and can be {{c2::inhaled}}.
Natural sources account for {{c1::most}} of background radiation exposure.
A 20-image full-mouth series taken with F-speed receptors and rectangular collimation is equivalent to {{c1::1–2 days}} of background radiation.
cloze.extra: Book: "20-film … F-speed films"; the exam no longer uses the word film.

cloze.text: The majority of artificial radiation exposure comes from {{c1::medical}} (not dental) assessments.
Dental radiation is responsible for {{c1::1–5}}% of the total exposure from medical imaging.
Dental radiographic exposure is similar to the dose received during a {{c1::cross-country airplane flight}}.
Other artificial radiation sources include {{c1::television}}, {{c2::smoke alarms}}, and building materials.
Filtration places absorbent materials, usually {{c1::aluminum}} discs, in the path of the X-rays to filter out {{c2::longer, non-productive}} wavelengths.
Filtration improves the {{c1::quality}} of the radiograph, reduces patient {{c2::dose}}, and decreases {{c3::scatter}}.
{{c1::Inherent}} filtration is built into the machine and includes the glass tube, oil, and {{c2::0.5–2}} mm of aluminum disks.
{{c1::Total}} filtration = inherent filtration + added filtration.
The PID is an open-ended {{c1::cylinder or rectangular}} device attached to the X-ray tube head that guides and {{c2::collimates}} the primary beam toward the patient.
The inside of the PID is lined with a {{c1::metallic}} layer to restrict the primary beam.
Standard PID lengths are {{c1::8}} inches and {{c2::16}} inches.
{{c1::Long (16-inch)}} PIDs produce more {{c2::parallel}} rays and reduce radiation exposure.
A {{c1::rectangular, lead-lined}} PID offers the greatest reduction of radiation exposure to the patient.
A collimator is a {{c1::metal}} barrier with an opening in the middle that restricts the size and shape of the X-ray beam.
Collimation reduces image {{c1::fog}}, improves image quality, and restricts patient exposure (primary and scattered).
cloze.extra: Book: "film fog" — the exam says image/radiograph.

cloze.text: Lead aprons of {{c1::0.25–3}} mm lead or lead equivalent protect patients from non-productive {{c2::scatter}} radiation.
The thyroid should always be protected by a {{c1::thyroid collar}}; the thyroid gland, particularly in {{c2::children}}, is one of the most radiosensitive organs.
Digital receptors require {{c1::50–90}}% less radiation exposure than film.
Beam alignment devices are placed in the patient's mouth with a portion toward the X-ray tube; they help achieve a better {{c1::paralleling}} technique.
A {{c1::dosimeter}} is a badge that measures the radiation exposure of the operator; it is worn at the {{c2::waist}}.
ALARA = {{c1::As Low As Reasonably Achievable}}: exposure should be kept to a minimum, and the {{c2::benefits}} should outweigh the risks for the patient.

basic.back: The propagation of energy through space in the form of particles or waves
The process by which an atom gains or loses electrons to become a negatively or positively charged atom
A charged particle that is either positive or negative
The force that moves electrons from the cathode to the anode
The precise area on the tungsten target where X-rays originate (electrons are directed there by the focusing cup)
Release of electrons by the heated (tungsten) filament when the power switch is activated, creating an electron cloud around the filament
Electrons are attracted toward the positive nucleus (opposite charges) and slow down (brake); the energy they lose is released as photons.
The time between radiation exposure and the observed clinical effect
A natural repair period in which most low-dose radiation injuries are repaired by the body
Radiation encountered in daily living, arising from natural and artificial sources

basic.front: Besides improving the paralleling technique, how do beam alignment devices reduce exposure?
basic.back: The device holds the receptor, so the patient's hand is not in the beam.

mcq.question: Which electron shell has the strongest binding energy?
mcq.explanation: The K shell is closest to the nucleus, so its electrons are held most tightly (highest binding energy). Binding energy decreases outward (L, M … Q), so the Q shell is the weakest.

mcq.question: Which statement about X-rays is correct?
options: A. They have a small mass and a negative charge
B. They have a long wavelength and low frequency
C. They travel at the speed of light and have no mass or charge
D. They are particulate radiation that travels in straight lines
mcq.answer: C. They travel at the speed of light and have no mass or charge
mcq.explanation: X-rays are electromagnetic: invisible, no mass, no charge, speed of light, high frequency and short wavelength. Particulate radiation (particles with mass) cannot reach the speed of light.

mcq.question: Which control-panel setting determines the penetrating power (quality) of the X-ray beam?
mcq.explanation: kVp sets the speed of the electrons and therefore the penetrating power (quality) of the beam. mA sets the NUMBER of electrons (quantity), not their energy.

mcq.question: Which tube-head component removes long, low-energy wavelengths that would only add to patient dose?
mcq.explanation: Aluminum disks filter out the soft (long, weak) wavelengths. The collimator does reduce exposure too, but by restricting the size and shape of the beam, not by filtering wavelengths.

mcq.question: Most of the X-rays produced in a dental tube result from:
mcq.explanation: About 70% of dental X-rays are braking radiation: electrons slowed by the tungsten nuclei. Characteristic radiation (inner-shell electrons dislodged) is a minor source; thermionic emission produces electrons, not X-rays.

mcq.question: In which interaction is the X-ray photon completely absorbed after ejecting an inner-shell electron?
mcq.explanation: In the photoelectric effect the photon hits an inner-shell electron and gives up all its energy. In Compton scatter the photon hits an outer-shell electron and keeps travelling with less energy.

mcq.question: Which interaction of X-rays with matter does NOT produce ionization?
mcq.explanation: In coherent scatter the photon continues with no energy loss and no electron is ejected, so no ionization occurs. Compton and photoelectric interactions both eject an electron (ionization).

mcq.question: Which SI unit expresses the absorbed dose adjusted for the biological damage potential of the radiation type?
mcq.explanation: Dose equivalent is measured in sieverts (SI) or rem (standard). The gray measures absorbed dose without the biological adjustment.

mcq.question: Most radiation-induced biologic damage occurs because radiation:
options: B. Ionizes water, forming free radicals and toxins
D. Causes coherent scatter in cells
mcq.answer: B. Ionizes water, forming free radicals and toxins
mcq.explanation: The indirect theory (≈2/3 of damage) — the body is 60–80% water, and free radicals (H, OH) form toxins such as hydrogen peroxide. Direct damage to DNA and other molecules accounts for only ≈1/3.

mcq.question: A higher radiation dose increases the chance that cancer develops, but not how severe the cancer is once it develops. This describes which type of effect?
mcq.explanation: Stochastic effects are all-or-none: dose changes the probability, not the severity. In deterministic (non-stochastic) effects such as hair loss, severity rises with dose above a threshold.

mcq.question: Which single change gives the greatest reduction in radiation exposure to the patient?
options: A. Switching from a 16-inch to an 8-inch PID
B. Using a rectangular, lead-lined PID
mcq.answer: B. Using a rectangular, lead-lined PID
mcq.explanation: A rectangular lead-lined PID gives the greatest reduction (rectangular collimation exposes 60% less tissue than round). Shortening the PID makes rays less parallel, and removing filtration leaves soft wavelengths that only add dose.

mcq.question: A hygienist wants to reduce scatter radiation and improve image quality. Which of these does BOTH?
mcq.explanation: Collimation restricts the size and shape of the beam, so less tissue is exposed, there is less scatter, less image fog and a better image. Removing filtration would increase patient dose.
